Title: Dynamic lead time coordination in supply chains under bilateral operational information asymmetry
Authors: Emma Salatiello, Francesca Papa, Silvestro Vespoli, Andrea Grassi
Abstract: Coordinating modern supply chains (SCs) is hindered by market volatility and, critically, by bilateral operational information asymmetry, where partners hold private, unverifiable information about their real-time capabilities. This study addresses this challenge by developing and testing a novel coordination framework for a dyadic SC, centered on a dynamic lead time negotiation coupled with an adaptive revenue-sharing mechanism. A comparative simulation analysis reveaals that while lead time negotiation alone enhances responsiveness by significantly reducing delivery times, it can paradoxically destroy total SC profit in decentralized settings due to uncompensated operational costs. However, the proposed integrated framework—combining negotiation with adaptive revenue sharing—proves highly effective. It not only fosters cooperation but also recovers nearly all profit losses from decentralization, while ensuring an equitable profit distribution. Furthermore, the study uncovers a critical insight into pricing power: a leader’s ability to charge for faster service is fundamentally limited by the partner’s economic viability, with a clear threshold beyond which an aggressive pricing strategy becomes value-destructive for the entire SC. This research contributes a novel operational contract that effectively mitigates the impacts of information asymmetry and enhances system-wide efficiency by explicitly linking dynamic operational decisions (lead time) to their shared financial consequences, offering a practical path toward resilient and profitable SC collaboration.

Title: Cooperative green innovation in platform supply chains under asymmetric market information
Authors: Jianghua Wu, Yinuo Zhao
Abstract: Amid the growing emphasis on corporate environmental responsibility, some e-commerce platforms provide financial support to help manufacturers invest in green product development. This study examines cooperative green innovation through cost-sharing within a platform supply chain considering both selling mode choices and asymmetric market information. A game-theoretic framework is employed to analyze mechanisms influencing manufacturers' green investment decisions, the platform's optimal cost-sharing strategy, and choices of selling modes and information-sharing strategies. First, our analysis demonstrates that platform-enabled information sharing facilitates manufacturers in aligning greenness with realized demand, thereby amplifying the value of information disclosure. Contrary to conventional wisdom, by strategically augmenting its green cost-sharing proportion, the platform may have an incentive for voluntary information disclosure under the reselling mode. This incentive intensifies as consumer green awareness rises. Second, with low greenness competition intensity, the platform's willingness to undertake green cost-sharing increases with price competition intensity, and agency mode is more advantageous for sharing green costs than reselling when the commission rate is high. Third, higher green cost-sharing proportions and greater consumer green awareness enhance the platform's incentive to adopt the agency mode. Specifically, when consumer green awareness is high and the platform bears a substantial share of green investment costs, the agency mode with information sharing leads to a win-win outcome under weak price competition; in contrast, the reselling mode with information sharing is mutually beneficial under intense price competition. This study provides significant managerial insights into collaborative green research and development operations within platform supply chains.

Title: Fine-tuning collaboration in a Co-opetitive manufacturing supply chain
Authors: Baozhuang Niu, Chencan Lin, Fengfeng Xie, Jianhua Zhang
Abstract: In recent years, fine-tuned Large Language Models (LLMs) have become increasingly important in manufacturers' improvement of production processes. Because of the heavy fine-tuning cost burden, firms within a supply chain have been witnessed to engage in fine-tuning collaboration, sharing efforts and results to reduce costs. Such collaboration, however, raises concerns about free-riding problems, which can be very typical in a co-opetitive supply chain. Therefore, we examine a manufacturing system including a supplier with self-brand and a manufacturer who both deploy their LLMs in production and make efforts on fine-tuning. We reveal that a higher intensity of fine-tuning collaboration creates a “suppression effect” which hampers stakeholders’ fine-tuning efforts out of the free-riding problems, and simultaneously a “synergy effect” which indicates that the overall market potential can be expanded by fine-tuning effort spillover, motivating them to invest more in fine-tuning. Driven by the dueling effects, the benefits of both the supplier and the manufacturer from fine-tuning collaboration exhibit non-monotonic relationships with respect to the collaboration intensity and the base product quality of the supplier. We further show that fine-tuning collaboration generally benefits the supplier more than the manufacturer in the co-opetitive relationship. Their incentives for collaboration are aligned if both the base product quality of the supplier and the collaboration intensity are relatively high.

Title: Hierarchical configuration decisions in transfer line balancing: Operational, tactical, and strategic effects on cycle time
Authors: Pedram Beldar, Amir Nourmohammadi, Masood Fathi, Amos H.C. Ng
Abstract: The Transfer Line Balancing Problem (TLBP) concerns the optimal assignment of tasks to workstations in automated machining lines to improve operational efficiency. This problem is particularly relevant to high-volume manufacturing industries, such as the automotive and aerospace industries, because it directly affects productivity and cost efficiency. This study examines how hierarchical configuration decisions at the operational (task assignment), tactical (joint task–tool assignment), and strategic (joint task–tool–fixture assignment) levels affect cycle time in an existing automotive machining transfer line. Three mixed-integer linear programming (MILP) models are developed to represent these configuration levels while accounting for setup times and industrial constraints, including task–machine accessibility, zoning, and technological restrictions. Because the exact models do not scale effectively to large instances, a constructive heuristic combined with a local search strategy is also developed. The proposed solution methods are evaluated using an industrial case study and 225 benchmark instances generated using a MILP-based benchmark generator. Across the benchmark size groups, operational cycle times are, on average, up to 11.87% and 12.65% higher than those obtained under tactical and strategic configurations, respectively, indicating potential productivity and economic benefits. The findings support managers in selecting an appropriate configuration level. Sensitivity analyses are also conducted to assess the effects of task–machine accessibility and task-time variability on solution performance.

Title: From scores to decision: Unveiling company maturity for Industry 4.0 using Benefit-of-the-Doubt models
Authors: Hermilio Vilarinho, André Guimarães, Eduardo e Oliveira, Teresa Pereira
Abstract: Digital maturity assessments are essential for guiding industrial firms through their transformation toward Industry 4.0. This study proposes a novel composite indicator to evaluate digital maturity using a Benefit-of-the-Doubt (BoD) approach grounded in robust and conditional efficiency techniques. Leveraging a unique dataset of 490 Portuguese firms that completed a self-assessment, following the IMPULS model adapted to the Portuguese context, we constructed firm-specific scores that account for performance heterogeneity and environmental factors. The empirical results show that firms exhibit low maturity in Smart Infrastructure, Smart Products, and Data-Driven Services, while Human Resources emerges as the comparatively most developed dimension, indicating that digital transformation remains at an early stage for most firms, especially SMEs. Importantly, this work pioneers the application of Generalized Additive Models (GAMs) to explore the non-linear influence of contextual variables, such as firm size, sector, and region, on digital maturity scores obtained via the BoD methodology. We find that conditional BoD scores differ significantly from the standard BoD and the fixed-weight IMPULS-adapted index, and that firm age category and sector exert significant effects on digital maturity, whereas financial productivity indicators do not. This innovative use of GAMs provides richer and more flexible insights than traditional parametric methods, uncovering complex interactions that affect firms’ digital maturity. Our findings offer actionable guidance for policymakers and industry stakeholders, highlighting priority areas for tailored support and capacity-building interventions. The proposed framework contributes both methodologically and empirically to the evaluation of Industry 4.0 maturity and provides a replicable approach for assessing digital transformation in other national and sectoral contexts.

Title: A supply chain digital twin for adaptive master planning under multi-source disruptions: Evidence from a dual-channel manufacturing case
Authors: Ali Rouzkhosh, S. Ali Torabi, Ali Beiki Ashkezari, Amir Ghasemi
Abstract: Conventional Supply Chain Master Planning (SCMP) approaches are poorly suited to environments characterized by simultaneous supply, demand, and sales-channel disruptions particularly in dual-channel supply chains where asymmetric shifts between online and offline demand can create inventory misallocation, service deterioration, and cost escalation. Although Supply Chain Digital Twins (SCDTs) are increasingly discussed as enablers of disruption-aware planning, limited evidence exists on how SCDT frameworks support adaptive SCMP in multi-echelon dual-channel settings. This study develops a SCDT framework for adaptive SCMP that integrates demand forecasting, machine learning-based disruption detection, discrete-event simulation, and multi-objective optimization to dynamically revise sourcing, production, and inventory decisions in response to evolving system states. The framework is instantiated in a television manufacturing supply chain and evaluated against static and rolling-horizon planning approaches under supplier, demand, and channel-shift disruptions. Results show that the proposed SCDT improves service-cost performance, supports more balanced channel-level fulfillment, and enhances adaptive recovery behavior under disruption relative to benchmark approaches. The findings further show that channel-aware SCMP is especially important when demand shifts asymmetrically across sales channels.

Title: Robotic assembly line balancing with on-site renewable energy supply
Authors: Yuchen Li, Francisco Saldanha-da-Gama, Ibrahim Kucukkoc, Dan Liu
Abstract: In this paper, a multi-criteria robotic assembly line balancing problem is integrated with long-term aggregate energy supply decisions. Three objectives are considered: production efficiency, carbon footprint, and cost. On-site renewable energy generation is assumed as an alternative to energy supply from the main grid. Two technologies are available: photovoltaic and wind power. To capture the uncertainty intrinsic to such energy output, a constraint is considered that imposes an energy supply feasibility margin. A deep Q-learning algorithm enhanced with fixed Q-target mechanisms and experience replay is proposed to find approximate Pareto-optimal solutions to the problem. Using a set of synthetic instances, this procedure is compared with a well-established metaheuristic. Additionally, an empirical case study, based on data from a manufacturing enterprise planning the long-term production of a specific engine type, is conducted to validate the proposed modeling framework and solution procedure. The results provide evidence that the methodological developments proposed can effectively inform the decision-making process, contributing to improved sustainability and operational performance in a production system.

Title: Risk assessment of relief food delivery delays from a cross-disaster perspective
Authors: Manyi Yang, Shao jian Qu, Zhuohua Qu, Rameshwar Dubey, Guoqing Zhao, Massoud Mohsendokht, Ying Ji, Zaili Yang
Abstract: Delays in relief food delivery critically threaten post-disaster survival, yet existing studies lack a systematic approach to identifying and assessing these risk factors across different disaster contexts. Focusing on floods and storms, this study develops a two-stage risk analysis framework tailored to relief food delivery delay risks across disaster contexts. Using multi-source real-world data and grounded theory, it identifies 24 risk factors, including previously overlooked institutional political risks such as geopolitical conflicts, political considerations, and bureaucratic approval redundancy. Methodologically, this study integrates failure mode and effect analysis (FMEA), a belief-rule-based Bayesian network, and evidential reasoning to assess and prioritise risks, while employing spherical fuzzy set-based social network analysis and the best-worst method to determine expert and risk factor weights. The results show that the key risk factors differ between disaster types: bureaucratic approval redundancy, traffic paralysis, and concentrated warehouse distribution dominate in floods; severe weather, bureaucratic approval redundancy, and communication infrastructure breakdown prevail in storms. This study contributes to delay risk assessment by applying an integrated FMEA–BBN–ER framework to the underexplored context of relief food delivery under floods and storms, while refining its weighting architecture through combined background–SFS–SNA expert weighting and BWM-based risk factor weighting to account for expert and risk factor heterogeneity. It further provides disaster-specific insights by cautiously interpreting how contextual factors, including governance capacity, institutional settings, and cultural value orientations, may help explain these differences and inform targeted mitigation strategies.

Title: Rethinking manufacturer–dealer relationships for customer solutions: From a single to a portfolio of relationship modes
Authors: Johanna Luisa Knapp, Heiko Gebauer, Oliver Gassmann, Felix Wortmann
Abstract: ABSTRACT As manufacturers bundle products, services, and software into customer solutions, they need to rethink both customer and dealer relationships. Existing literature mainly explores changes in manufacturer-customer ties. Less is known about how manufacturers that use dealers as intermediaries for customer solutions must adapt their relationships with dealers. This article draws on an abductive qualitative study comprising 47 interviews with manufacturers, dealers, and customers across six industries, complemented by an embedded process case. The research examines how greater solution orientation reshapes manufacturer–dealer relationships. The findings reveal three relationship modes: (1) manufacturer-led enablement, (2) joint coordination, and (3) strategic co-creation. These modes differ in governance, coordination, decision-making, and power. The study extends the relational-process view of customer solutions to dealer-mediated channels. We develop the relationship mode portfolio concept and show that advanced servitization does not necessarily eliminate dealers; instead, dealers assume different roles depending on solution requirements.

Title: Operational metrics in derivatives adoption: Evidence from China's chemical industry
Authors: Wubo Zhang, Qi Zhang, Gangshu (George) Cai
Abstract: ABSTRACT Manufacturers face severe raw-material price volatility. Inventory represents both a core operational asset and their primary source of risk exposure. The operations-finance interface literature links these operational realities to financial hedging. However, large-sample evidence on what drives the decision remains scarce. Drawing on 289 listed Chinese chemical firms from 2016 to 2022, we address this gap. We examine how operational exposure, measured by inventory level and inventory turnover, compares against traditional financial determinants. Specifically, we evaluate their relative impact on firms’ derivations adoption. Our empirical strategy integrates probit estimation, moderation analysis, and k-means clustering. We find that operational metrics are the primary drivers of derivatives adoption. Inventory level and turnover outweigh traditional financial indicators, including liquidity, leverage, and growth. Among financial factors, only pre-tax profit remains consistently significant. Furthermore, the firm’s financial capacity moderates these effects. Operational exposure dominates the hedging decisions of cash-constrained firms. Conversely, well-capitalized firms hedge more selectively. These findings remain robust to rigorous endogeneity tests and controls for geographic heterogeneity and pandemic shocks. Building on these empirical patterns, we develop a managerial decision framework. This framework maps a firm’s operational exposure and financial capacity to specific hedging stances and derivative instruments. Finally, this study contributes large-sample empirical evidence on the relative importance of operational versus financial drivers of derivatives adoption, bridging the operations-finance interface with industrial practice.

Title: Farmer self-returning or outsourcing? An agricultural product supply chain network operation and straw returning mode selection strategies
Authors: Caiquan Duan, Shan Liu, Fengmin Yao, Yan Sun
Abstract: Ensuring sustainable operation of agricultural product supply chain networks while safeguarding cultivated land is essential to advancing agricultural green transformation. This study integrates straw returning into an agricultural product supply chain network, recognizing its role in enhancing soil organic matter and reducing reliance on chemical fertilizer. Drawing on noncooperative game theory and variational inequality, an agricultural product supply chain network equilibrium model is developed under two straw returning modes: farmer self-returning and outsourcing returning. The equilibrium results and straw returning mode selection strategies are explored under the influence of single- and dual-factor scenarios, including straw returning subsidy, outsourcing fee, chemical fertilizer cost, under-fulfillment penalty, and straw nutrient release rate. Results show that increases in the other factors generally promote the returning rate under both returning modes, whereas an increase in the straw nutrient release rate does not boost the returning rate under the outsourcing mode. However, their impacts on profits differ significantly. Comparative analyses indicate that both farmers and retailers gain greater profits when straw returning is implemented by other-tier entities. Nevertheless, the preferable straw returning mode in terms of whole system profits and the straw returning rate mainly depends on the interactions among the above factors. Notably, the outsourcing returning mode proves to be the more viable strategy for achieving a win-win situation between whole system profits and cultivated land protection in most scenarios. In contrast, only when the subsidy level is low and the chemical fertilizer cost is high does the self-returning mode become the dominant strategy.

Title: Joint product-service innovation in EV battery-swapping supply chains under alternative service leadership structures: Insights from the Chinese market
Authors: Qiuting Li, Ying Li, Feifan Li
Abstract: With the rapid diffusion of electric vehicles, battery-swapping has emerged as a replenishment alternative that converts time savings into potential market adoption. Battery-swapping represents a product-service system, whose diffusion hinges on complementary innovations between product-side compatibility and service-side capacity. As battery-swapping networks attract investment from battery suppliers, vehicle manufacturers, and third-party firms, differences in capital commitment and control over service assets bring service leadership structures to the forefront of strategic analysis. Accordingly, we investigate product-service innovation and pricing decisions under three leadership regimes, and examine equity-based coordination through cross-shareholding. To capture demand heterogeneity arising from time-based competition between charging and swapping, we develop a circular Hotelling model of a swapping supply chain comprising a battery supplier, a manufacturer, and a service provider. Our results highlight three key findings. First, higher users time value generally expands swapping adoption under decentralized leadership, but may reduce adoption when the manufacturer self-operates service, unless coordination efficiency is sufficiently high. Second, leadership advantages are stage contingent. When time advantages and differentiation are strong, regimes that better internalize cross-stage gains achieve higher innovation levels, lower effective service prices, and greater penetration; as fast charging technologies converge and substitution intensifies, performance becomes increasingly sensitive to cost efficiency and asset turnover. Third, cross-shareholding can mitigate innovation spillovers and improve both supply-chain performance and consumer welfare, but its incentive effects depend on leadership structure: under third-party leadership, innovation is inverted-U in equity intensity, whereas under supplier leadership, stronger equity alignment more consistently promotes innovation, particularly in time-sensitive markets.

Title: The value of advance demand information for shipment consolidation under customer behavioral responses
Authors: Haiwei Lu, Gudrun P. Kiesmüller
Abstract: This paper studies how warehouses should price advance demand information to maximize its value in shipment consolidation systems. Unlike existing research that assumes exogenous demand, we explicitly model customer ordering behavior as influenced by discount rates, delivery lead times, and order cancellation risks. We develop three shipment consolidation policies: a Bayesian-optimized approximate threshold policy, a layered decision policy, and a cost-based myopic policy, to determine optimal discount rates under various operational conditions. Numerical experiments demonstrate that the layered policy achieves near-optimal performance with only 0.05% average optimality gap. Our analysis reveals that optimal discount rates exhibit an inverted-U relationship with demand lead time. Price sensitivity significantly amplifies optimal discounts, while high cancellation costs and severe late-delivery penalties constrain discount strategies. In addition, incorporating cancellation behavior significantly improves system performance. These findings provide actionable guidance for pricing advance demand information through discount strategies under different operational conditions.

Title: Worker skill assessment in human-centric assembly systems
Authors: Angela Lago Alvarez, Wael M. Mohammed, Jose Luis Martinez Lastra
Abstract: : Accurate assessment of human worker skills is essential for human-centric automation in modern manufacturing systems. However, modelling these skills remains challenging due to variability in human performance and limited high-quality open-access datasets. This study proposes an approach for evaluating individual worker skill levels in assembly systems and assessing the reliability of internal company metrics. It introduces worker-specific learning curves that capture individual skill progression through an exponential model that incorporates three parameters: , representing worker-specific learning rate, , quantifying previous experience and, , correcting inaccuracies in the NMV (Nominal Measured Value) calculations or pre-training effects. An algorithm based on the trust-region method is used to fit the model using task execution data, effectively capturing individualized learning trajectories and distinguishing skill progression across workers. The proposed approach was validated using a real dataset collected from an assembly line over two weeks, where four workers performed tasks at both manual and collaborative workstations. As this dataset can be seen insufficient, a Moving Block Bootstrap (MBB) stability analysis was conducted to assess the robustness of the fitted learning curve parameters under resampling. The MBB results show partial stability, with some parameters remaining consistent under resampling while others vary more substantially. Comparison with company-reported skill levels reveals notable discrepancies, highlighting the need for improved assessment methodologies. Furthermore, the proposed approach was benchmarked against classical learning curve models. The dataset is released as open-access, enabling transparent and reproducible research and fostering advancements in skill modelling.

Title: Unleashing the value of resource orchestration: How supply chain finance enhances corporate ESG performance
Authors: Qiang Lu, Kemu Su, Yudong Yang, Zhongqi Yu
Abstract: Enhancing corporate ESG performance has emerged as a strategic priority for businesses worldwide. However, regardless of whether ESG initiatives stem from regulatory compliance or proactive sustainability commitments, their implementation frequently confronts significant resource constraints. Against this backdrop, this study investigates how supply chain finance (SCF) can serve as an innovative tool for resource orchestration to improve corporate ESG performance. Grounded in resource orchestration theory (ROT), this study elucidates how SCF integrates internal and external organizational resources and transforms them into the key capabilities necessary for the implementation of sustainable strategies, constructing a triple-capability mechanism framework. Drawing on data from Chinese A-share listed companies between 2012 and 2024, this study employs a fixed-effects regression model that accounts for both firm- and year-specific effects to test the proposed research hypotheses. The empirical analysis demonstrates a significantly positive association between SCF and corporate ESG performance. Moreover, this relationship can be mediated by overall operation capability (OOC), green innovation capability (GIC), and social responsibility capability (SRC). Further analysis examines the conditional roles of digitalization and supply chain characteristics as key contextual factors. It indicates that both digital transformation (DT) and artificial intelligence (AI) adoption positively moderate the effects of SCF on OOC and GIC, while showing no significant influence on the relationship between SCF and SRC. Supply chain concentration (SCC) significantly strengthens the impact of SCF on OOC, yet it negatively moderates the relationships between SCF, GIC and SRC. In contrast, the quality of supply chain relationship (SCR) does not affect the SCF–OOC link, but significantly enhances the relationships between SCF and both GIC and SRC.

Title: Embedding resilience in biological production through functional modularity: A mixed-method approach
Authors: Huynh Thi Ngoc Diep, Ho Huy Tuu, Nguyen Thi Tram Anh
Abstract: Resilience is commonly conceptualised as a capability developed in response to disruption rather than as a property embedded in a production organisation. Drawing on evidence from biological production, specifically the shrimp-farming context in Vietnam, this study identifies a recurring structural pattern reflecting the core principles of modularity and explains how it enables resilience to emerge endogenously from the production structure. A sequential mixed-methods design combines an in-depth case study, which uncovers the organisational mechanisms through which modular structures isolate disturbances, enable functional substitution, and support adaptive recombination, with a quasi-experimental analysis that provides causal evidence of their contribution to production continuity during pandemic disruptions. The findings show that resilience is generated by the structural organisation of production while simultaneously improving operational efficiency. The study advances resilience theory by demonstrating how resilience emerges as an endogenous property of production organisation and clarifying the mechanisms through which modularity generates resilience.

Title: Reconstruction of intertemporal pricing competition in two-sided markets based on fairness concerns
Authors: Dingbo Tan, Qingmei Tan, Kebing Chen
Abstract: Digital subscription platforms such as Netflix and iQiyi frequently employ dynamic pricing, and users naturally perceive fairness concerns in response to such price changes. These fairness concerns significantly influence the equilibrium pricing structures of two-sided subscription platforms. This paper develops a two-period dynamic pricing game model to study how buyers' fairness concerns alter the platforms' pricing structure across buyers and sellers. We show that fairness concerns demonstrate flexibility in adjusting pricing strategies in the intertemporal game of two-sided markets. Different from previous studies, the side with stronger network effects will be subsidized rather than subject to more aggressive pricing decisions when fairness concerns are low. Furthermore, the platform's pricing strategy is jointly determined by retention rates and fairness concerns. Specifically, for buyers, the platforms adopt the ‘ penetration-harvesting ’ strategy when both the retention rate and fairness concerns are weak. However, if the retention rate is high, the ‘lock-in effect’ will be utilized to increase the price. For sellers, the platforms adopt an incremental pricing mechanism. We also find that the buyers' fairness concerns can lead to asymmetric pricing adoption, which alters the traditional seesaw effect (where price increases on one side correspond to decreases on the other). Additionally, the unit transportation cost of two-sided users and fairness concerns jointly determine the strategy selection of the platforms. Essentially, in two-sided markets with strong network externalities, moderate fairness concerns can enhance social welfare.

Title: Strategic information sharing in platform-based consumer-to-manufacturer customization
Authors: Qing Zhang, Yan Zhang, Yini Zheng, Yong He
Abstract: As consumer demand diversifies, consumer-to-manufacturer (C2M) customization has emerged as a new production paradigm. It leverages data collection and analysis of consumer preferences to inform the tailored product design and manufacturing. This paper investigates a platform-based C2M customization mode in which the platform can choose whether to share information to empower the manufacturer’s C2M customization production. By introducing a two-dimensional product matching framework that decomposes consumers’ matching preferences into functional matching and personalized matching, we examine the interplay between the manufacturer’s C2M customization and the platform’s information sharing strategy and investigate how the interaction impacts the supply chain members’ decisions and profits. We obtain several main results. Firstly, the platform’s information sharing does not consistently incentivize the manufacturer to invest in C2M customization, and may not always yield mutual benefits for both parties. Secondly, when the manufacturer’s C2M investment efficiency is low, the platform is more inclined to share consumer preference information with the manufacturer, thereby facilitating the manufacturer’s C2M customization investments at equilibrium. Conversely, the equilibrium strategy compels the manufacturer to collect consumer information to promote C2M customization, as the platform withholds information. Lastly, a win–win outcome occurs when the manufacturer’s C2M customization investment efficiency is not excessively high. We extend the model in several ways to verify robustness. Our findings provide managerial insights for manufacturers and platforms considering engagement in C2M customization.

Title: Supply chain complexity and innovation ambidexterity: Thresholds, role differentiation, and coordination regimes
Authors: Jingwei Xu, Fengwen Chen, Yinghua Shen
Abstract: Supply chain complexity reshapes firms’ innovation choices, yet its implications for innovation ambidexterity remain unclear. This study develops a biform game model to examine how complexity influences the balance between exploration and exploitation within and across firms. We show that complexity has a dual effect by expanding innovation opportunities while increasing coordination frictions. This trade-off generates threshold conditions under which within-firm ambidexterity becomes less sustainable and specialization becomes more attractive. Even so, the weakening of internal ambidexterity does not necessarily eliminate ambidexterity at the system level. Under heterogeneous participation conditions, role differentiation across firms can preserve an ambidextrous supply chain structure. We further show that coordination regimes, including standards, platforms, and integration investments, can mitigate frictions and shift these thresholds. Numerical analysis illustrates these patterns over a broader parameter range. The study extends research on innovation ambidexterity to complex interorganizational settings and offers implications for collaborative supply chain design.

Title: Differentiated vs. progressive carbon taxes: A comparative analysis in non-independent third-party remanufacturing
Authors: Xiqiang Xia, Peiying Wan, Senlin Zhao
Abstract: Remanufacturing has emerged as a critical strategy for addressing environmental challenges and advancing sustainable development. This study investigates the impact of two carbon tax policy instruments—Differentiated Carbon Tax (DCT) and Progressive Carbon Tax (PCT)—on non-independent third-party remanufacturing, specifically within the Authorized Remanufacturing Model (ARM) and the Outsourced Remanufacturing Model (ORM). Employing game theory, four models capturing the interactions between Original Equipment Manufacturers (OEMs) and Third-Party Remanufacturers (TPRs) are developed. Key findings derived from analytical and numerical analyses are: (1) Both DCT and PCT policies, when levied on OEMs, decrease NP sales. This decline indirectly stimulates demand for remanufactured products, fostering the expansion of the remanufacturing market. (2) Under both carbon tax regimes, the ORM outperforms the ARM in promoting end-of-life product collection. For OEMs, the ORM also generates superior economic benefits. (3) Neither carbon tax policy universally dominates the other under either remanufacturing model. The used product collection rate and the economic returns for supply chain participants are contingent upon the specific tax rates implemented within each policy framework.

Title: Behavior-based pricing of low-carbon products via data-driven pricing under cap-and-trade and subsidies
Authors: Kanying Liu, Wei Li
Abstract: We explore the necessity and feasibility of adopting behavior-based pricing (BBP) for low-carbon products under cap-and-trade based on consumer data, carbon emission reduction data, and carbon subsidy data. We construct a dynamic pricing game model covering the “data acquisition—application data (policy response)” process and investigate the implementation conditions, specific pathways, and welfare levels of data-driven BBP under different scenarios. We find that the poaching strategy of low-carbon manufacturers toward ordinary product consumers is comprehensively influenced by factors such as carbon price, emission reduction, carbon subsidies, and consumer low-carbon preferences. Low-carbon consumption subsidies can further expand the entrapment of potential consumers of low-carbon products. When there are no subsidies or when the subsidy intensity is low, uniform pricing is the dominant strategy for low-carbon manufacturers; when the subsidy intensity is strong, BBP becomes the dominant strategy for low-carbon manufacturers. BBP can expand the market share of low-carbon products, reduce total corporate carbon emissions, increase consumer surplus for low-carbon consumption groups, and improve overall social welfare; providing subsidies to low-carbon consumers under BBP can further amplify these effects.

Title: From augmentation to action: AI-LLM–enabled improvisation and reactive capability in digital manufacturing supply chains
Authors: Soumyadeb Chowdhury, Sachin Kumar Mangla, Guo Li
Abstract: Amid global disruptions and rapid technological change, digital manufacturing supply chains face growing pressure to develop reactive capabilities. This study examines the relationships among artificial intelligence large language model (AI-LLM) augmentation, supply chain improvisation, and reactive capability. Grounded in the dynamic capabilities view (DCV), we propose and empirically test a conceptual model in which supply chain improvisation mediates the association between AI-LLM augmentation and reactive capability, while digital innovation resistance and supply chain decisiveness act as moderators. Survey data from 224 UK supply chain managers were analysed using Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modelling (PLS-SEM). The results show that AI-LLM augmentation is positively associated with reactive capability via supply chain improvisation. Digital innovation resistance weakens the AI-LLM–improvisation relationship, underscoring the importance of an digital innovation-supportive culture, and supply chain decisiveness strengthens the relationship between improvisation and reactive capability, highlighting the value of prompt decision-making mechanisms. Overall, this study extends DCV by clarifying AI-LLM augmentation as a micro-foundational capability that supports improvisation in uncertain supply chain environments, and thus offers guidance for managers seeking to leverage AI-LLM augmentation to build reactive capabilities while managing resistance and fostering decisiveness in digital manufacturing supply chains.

Title: Editorial Board
Profitability transparency in power-imbalanced supply chains: Higher retailer payoffs, weaker relationship continuation
Authors: Guy Barokas, Oded Ravid, Nelly Bart
Abstract: Transparency is frequently advocated in supply chains because better information can reduce coordination failures and mitigate bargaining inefficiencies. Yet in power-imbalanced buyer–supplier relationships, disclosure can change what becomes salient in negotiation, shifting attention toward rents. We study whether profitability transparency can harm relationship quality and continuation when the upstream party has a strong outside option. In a pre-registered, incentivized online retailer–supplier bargaining experiment with stochastic demand and inventory risk (N = 200), retailers negotiate a wholesale price and order quantity against a supplier with an advantaged disagreement payoff. Retailers either observe the supplier's net unit cost (complete information) or receive only incomplete cost information that prevents precise inference and yields higher expected cost estimates (i.e., lower expected supplier profitability). As predicted, the economic and relational effects diverge: relative to complete information, incomplete information lowers the retailer's expected payoff implied by the negotiated agreement by 23.5%, yet significantly increases perceived fairness, satisfaction, and an incentivized measure of willingness to negotiate again. Conditioning on the retailer's payoff further amplifies the incomplete-information advantage in all three relational outcomes, consistent with a rent-salience channel in which evaluations depend on both own outcomes and inferred counterpart rents. The results tighten a boundary condition for transparency: when leverage is asymmetric, making upstream profitability transparent can carry relational costs that are operationally consequential for continuation. To preserve relationship quality, transparency initiatives may therefore require complements, such as gain-sharing rules or limits on how disclosed cost information is used.

Title: Operational readiness for responsible technological transformation in textile SMEs: A conceptual framework and maturity model to support sustainable decision-making in production environments
Authors: Israel Naranjo, Rocio de la Torre, Llanos Cuenca, Andrés Boza
Abstract: Textile SMEs are under pressure to adopt technologies that improve their operational efficiency, production visibility, resource allocation, and competitiveness, while also meeting demands for sustainability and responsible transformation. However, their financial constraints and lack of organizational readiness make this process difficult. This study proposes a conceptual framework to guide responsible technological transformation in textile SMEs, complemented with a decision-support maturity model (MM-RET 3 -SME) that links technology adoption to production efficiency, cost-related constraints, and sustainability-oriented performance. The framework details 20 internal and external driving forces classified into five categories, relevant Industry 4.0 technologies and defines 15 critical requirements in six categories. These elements are associated with operational readiness, cost-related constraints, and the conditions required for economically viable and responsible technological adoption. In addition, the proposed maturity model (Level 0–5) works as a decision-support tool for prioritizing investment actions according to maturity gaps. The research combines literature reviews, interviews with experts and a fuzzy analysis that validates the model and weights the criteria. The results show that: (i) the overall maturity level of the sector is at Level 2; (ii) enterprise size is a key factor, as the results place companies at different levels depending on their size: micro-enterprises (Level 1), small (Level 2) and medium-sized enterprises (Level 3); and (iii) the main gaps are in infrastructure and technology, data management, security and regulations, and costs and viability. From a production economics perspective, the model supports SMEs in linking technological readiness with investment prioritization, cost-related constraints, resource allocation, and operational performance under sustainability requirements.

Title: Competitive pricing and cooperation mode strategies on E-commerce platforms with reference price effect
Authors: Ningning Wang, Jing Li, Lin Wei
Abstract: Manufacturers are increasingly inclined to distribute products through multiple e-commerce platforms simultaneously. This trend provides strategic consumers with more opportunities to compare retail prices across different platforms, thereby generating a reference price effect. The manufacturer may cooperate with each platform under either an agency mode or a reselling mode. Besides, a uniform pricing or a differentiated pricing can be adopted. Motivated by this emerging practice, this paper investigates the competitive pricing and cooperation mode strategies by considering reference price effect. We focus on a platform-based supply chain comprising one manufacturer and two e-commerce platforms. The results indicate that: (i) From the perspective of manufacturer and platform profits, differentiated pricing is more preferable with unilateral reference price effect while uniform pricing can conditionally dominate differentiated pricing with cross reference price effect. (ii) A strong reference price effect can aggravate double marginalization under mode (R, A) but alleviate it under mode (A, R). Besides, it can mitigate platforms’ price competition between platforms with a low commission rate. (iii) When the commission rate is moderate, both reference price effect and platform competition jointly determine cooperation modes strategy. (iv) There exists a triple-win situation for the platform supply chain members. Our extended models indicate that the main findings are robust.

Title: Disruption-resilient lot-sizing and scheduling using multimodal deep reinforcement learning and distributionally robust evaluation
Authors: Mohammad Asghari, Mohamad Y. Jaber, Cory Searcy, Hamid Afshari
Abstract: Modern manufacturing systems face increasing pressure to remain cost-efficient, responsive, and resilient amid operational uncertainty and disruptive events. While traditional scheduling methods offer limited adaptability, existing AI-based solutions often overlook robustness and risk sensitivity in complex production settings. This study addresses this gap by developing a multimodal deep reinforcement learning (MDRL) framework that learns data-driven scheduling policies under routine stochastic variability and evaluates them through distributionally robust and tail-risk-based disruption stress tests. The proposed approach leverages a transformer-based algorithm enhanced with transformer encoders and cross-modal attention to processing diverse data sources. Robustness is assessed through scenario-based disruption stress testing and CVaR/DRO-based robustness scoring for post-training checkpoint selection. Experimental results reveal that the MDRL agent consistently favors mid-sized lot sizes (peaking around 58 units) and reduces setup activations by approximately 30%, promoting stable and efficient operations. Analyses for robustness show that while increasing the CVaR threshold from 0.5 to 0.99 raises worst-case cost by over 50%, it leads to a 26% drop in service level, highlighting critical trade-offs between risk aversion and responsiveness. These findings highlight the potential of MDRL to optimize operational performance while supporting systematic robustness evaluation in real-time production environments. The framework offers a scalable and intelligent decision-making tool for next-generation smart factories, with implications for operational efficiency, sustainability, and supply chain resilience.

Title: Resilient supplier selection and order allocation under disruption risk over a Wasserstein ambiguity
Authors: Xin Li, Xuan Vinh Doan, Juergen Branke
Abstract: Supply chain resilience is increasingly important for safeguarding operations against disruption risk, presenting decision-makers with the challenge of balancing cost efficiency and effective risk mitigation. We study the problem of resilient supplier selection and order allocation under uncertain disruption impact. Probability distributions of the actual disruption impact are unknown, and only a possibly small set of historical realizations may be available. To handle the distributional uncertainty, we first construct an ambiguity set that encompasses all possible distributions of disruption impact within a 1-Wasserstein distance from the empirical distribution. We then define a two-stage distributionally robust supplier selection and order allocation problem to determine optimal sourcing and contingency decisions among available suppliers under capacity constraints. The objective is to minimize the total cost consisting of the fixed cost related to contracting suppliers plus the worst-case mean-CVaR associated with disruption over all distributions defined in the ambiguity set. Using the model structural properties, we derive a mixed-integer linear programming (MILP) reformulation that can be implemented and solved using off-the-shelf optimization software. We conduct numerical experiments based on synthetic data inspired by a real-world case taken from the literature. The experiment results demonstrate that our proposed model yields robust solutions and achieves superior out-of-sample performance over the stochastic approach.

Title: Research on China's new energy vehicles industry chain game under tariff uncertainty
Authors: Yanxin Liu, Haoyu Wang, Xin Cai
Abstract: As geopolitical risks continue to escalate, the new energy vehicle (NEV) industry chain has become increasingly exposed to tariff shocks across multiple segments. This study develops a three-party dynamic game model based on international market game, incorporating four tariff scenarios and five bargaining power settings to analyze firms' optimal strategies. The results show that the combination of low costs for integrated firms and high costs for final product firm can generate a win–win outcome for domestic firms. Bargaining power exerts a positive effect on the prices of intermediate goods, and such effects vary distinctly under different game structures. Under the output sequential game, stronger bargaining power benefits integrated firms while reducing downstream firms’ profits. In contrast, under the price simultaneous game, stronger bargaining power benefits the profits of all firms increase simultaneously. From the perspective of national profits, the optimal strategy under the output sequential game is characterized by low tariffs, high final product costs, and low bargaining power, whereas the price simultaneous game favors high tariffs, low intermediate product costs, and high bargaining power. Although cost declines of foreign firms tend to erode the profit levels of domestic firms, excessively high tariffs can yield localization-related benefits. These findings suggest that tariff and bargaining strategies could be adjusted according to different game structures to improve domestic industrial competitiveness.

Title: Industrial internet platform–enabled supply chain low-carbon transformation: A two-stage evolutionary game approach
Authors: Xiang Li, Zibo Lin, Yu Cao
Abstract: Climate change mitigation and net-zero targets have increased the pressure on manufacturing supply chains to reduce carbon emissions across organizational boundaries. However, supply-chain-wide low-carbon transformation remains difficult because focal firms have limited governance reach over multi-tier partners, while many small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) face capability and resource constraints. Industrial Internet Platforms (IIPs) provide a potential mechanism for addressing this challenge by transforming localized low-carbon practices into reusable modules and supporting their diffusion across supply chain networks. This study develops a two-stage evolutionary game framework to examine IIP-enabled supply chain low-carbon transformation. Stage I models a tripartite evolutionary game among the IIP, focal firms, and affiliated firms, capturing the joint evolution of low-carbon module construction, focal-firm cooperation, and affiliated-firm transformation. Stage II embeds SMEs in a scale-free network to analyze how the platform capabilities formed in Stage I affect the diffusion of low-carbon modules. The results reveal three main findings. First, stable low-carbon transformation depends on the coordinated formation of platform-enabled capabilities: stronger capability building in Stage I accelerates and stabilizes SME adoption in Stage II, whereas partial cooperation leads only to limited or fragmented transformation. Second, government policies have nonlinear and stage-dependent effects. A coordinated portfolio of subsidies, penalties, and tax incentives can reduce module-construction and transformation costs, thereby promoting the formation of a robust low-carbon capability system. Third, network structure significantly shapes diffusion outcomes. Larger networks provide more redundant diffusion paths and facilitate broader adoption, whereas excessive clustering creates information redundancy and slows convergence. This study contributes to low-carbon supply chain research by linking platform-enabled capability building with network diffusion, extends platform governance research by conceptualizing low-carbon modules as endogenous capabilities, and offers implications for policy design and supply chain management practice.

Title: Cash or upgrade? Trade-in and remanufacturing strategies in a dual-market e-platform supply chain
Authors: Kebing Chen, Hui Wang, Ginger Y. Ke
Abstract: Trade-in-for-upgrade (TU) and trade-in-for-cash (TC) programs have been widely adopted to generate economic and environmental benefits. Despite the existing efforts in investigating how trade-in programs stimulate product sales and facilitate used-product recovery, their applications in e-platform closed-loop supply chains (ECLSCs) remain insufficiently explored. In particular, limited attention has been paid to ECLSCs with coexisting new and secondhand markets under different online modes. Motivated by this gap, this paper investigates trade-in programs in an ECLSC under resale and agency modes by considering TU-only, TC-only, and TU-TC coexistence settings. The results show that trade-in programs influence product recovery, remanufacturing decisions, and competition between new and secondhand products. Moreover, the TU-TC coexistence setting is always beneficial to the trade-in implementer, whereas its impact on the other member depends on the online mode, equilibrium strategy, and production cost of new products. In addition, resale and agency modes may achieve preference alignment between ECLSC members and consumers under certain conditions.

Title: Unlocking the catastrophe mechanism in fresh produce E-commerce supply chain coalitions: An integration of stochastic evolutionary game and catastrophe theory
Authors: Xiaochao Wei, Yanfei Zhang
Abstract: The rapid growth of fresh produce e-commerce platforms has prompted the formation of dynamic supply chain coalitions to improve efficiency and reduce costs. However, these coalitions face significant challenges under uncertainty, resulting in abrupt disruptions, yet their dynamic evolution, driven by stochastic strategic interactions and nonlinear regime shifts, remains underexplored. Accordingly, we develop a stochastic catastrophe model to explore such abrupt changes by combining the stochastic evolutionary game (SEG) and catastrophe theory. Specifically, we employ an SEG with Gaussian white noise to model asymmetric strategic interactions between fresh e-commerce platforms and suppliers, then transform the replicator dynamics into a cusp catastrophe model. We mathematically derive the catastrophe threshold (i.e., singularity set) and distinguish two fundamentally different types: perturbation catastrophes triggered by external shocks, and structural catastrophes arising from gradual internal imbalances. The coalition catastrophe can be accurately controlled by parameter adjustment to form the shortest path to avoid catastrophe (precatastrophe), delay catastrophe (in-catastrophe), and recover from catastrophe (postcatastrophe). Numerical simulations show that excess revenue π negatively impacts the stability of fresh produce e-commerce supply chain coalitions (FPESCCs), but value–freshness elasticity positively impacts FPESCC stability, and value–freshness level has an inverted U-shaped effect on the stability of FPESCCs. When the initial willingness to cooperate is low, a lower service-cost coefficient helps stabilize FPESCCs. Robustness checks using alternative functional forms and product heterogeneity confirm the qualitative stability of these findings. This integrated approach provides a new perspective for supply chain coalition research, offering quantitative insights for guiding policy optimization.

Title: Enabling empowerment over exploitative specialization: The role of total productive maintenance in precarious work contexts
Authors: Maria Joao Coelho Guedes, Mateus do Rego Ferreira Lima, Elliot Bendoly, Pankaj Patel, Daniel Bachrach
Abstract: The growing reliance on contingent workers raises critical questions about organizational practices that shape both firm performance and worker outcomes. We examine how high-performance work practices (HPWPs) focused on specialization versus empowerment influence contingent worker development, organizational returns, and risks of exploitation. We then compare these practices with the more organic, process-oriented principles of Total Productive Maintenance (TPM), emphasizing transparency, cross-training, and discretion as foundations that enable empowerment to deliver mutual benefits. We employ a multi-method, multi-source design: matched-sample surveys of operations and human resource (HR) managers, third-party financial data, and 14 semi-structured post-hoc interviews with HR and operations managers. Our results reveal two distinct paths for firms. A specialization-focused approach enhances task-specific productivity but risks limiting professional growth, with burdens falling on contingent workers. In contrast, when TPM conditions provide knowledge foundations, empowerment practices show a significant positive relationship with return on equity. Interviews further indicate that such empowerment benefits not only firms financially but also contingent workers’ professional well-being. This study highlights the dual-edged nature of HPWPs for contingent workers, distinguishing between potentially exploitative specialization and mutually beneficial empowerment. By demonstrating how TPM conditions enable empowerment to deliver both organizational and worker gains, we contribute to theory and practice on the sociotechnical dynamics of contingent work. Findings underscore the importance of coordinated operations and HR planning, showing that empowerment can only succeed when supported by transparent processes and cross-functional training.

Title: Strategic interactions of platform information sharing and supplier encroachment in a multi-tier supply chain
Authors: Nenggui Zhao, Jing Wang, Panpan Xia
Abstract: This paper considers a multi-tier supply chain comprising an online platform, a supplier, and a retailer. The platform possesses a market information advantage and decides whether to share this information with either the retailer or the supplier, thereby forming asymmetric and symmetric information structures. The supplier determines its encroachment and the sequence of sales quantity decisions, leading to three supply chain structures. Under asymmetric information structures, the uninformed player makes operational decisions based on signals transmitted by the informed player, resulting in signaling games. We develop a series of Stackelberg and signaling game models to examine the individual, joint, and mutual effects of encroachment, information sharing, and the sequence of quantity decisions on supply chain performance. The findings indicate that the platform consistently exhibits a willingness to share information with other players. A separating equilibrium is proved to be the optimal strategy under asymmetric information structures, except when the supplier refrains from encroachment. In such cases, players may distort information to achieve the separating equilibrium. The supplier can strategically adjust the sequence of sales quantity decisions, making encroachment beneficial for both itself and the platform while detrimental to the retailer. Additionally, if the supplier chooses to encroach, it will always determine sales quantity after the retailer has made its decision, which in turn compels the platform to fully share information with the other players. In such a case, a Nash equilibrium emerges between the platform and the supplier.

Title: Strategic interactions and operational efficiency in supply chain networks: A game-theoretic network directional distance function approach
Authors: Sheng-Wei Lin
Abstract: This study develops an integrated Game-Theoretic Network Directional Distance Function (DDF) framework that bridges the gap between operational efficiency measurement and strategic interaction analysis in complex supply chain networks. While existing literature treats these dimensions separately, our research demonstrates their fundamental interdependence through a novel methodology that combines network DDF models with game-theoretic analyses of competitive (Nash equilibrium) and cooperative (Shapley value) scenarios. Using comprehensive data from NVIDIA's supply chain network (53 firms across four tiers, 2018-2021), we uncover three critical findings. First, pervasive operational inefficiencies exist with 30-40% improvement potential across all tiers despite intense competition. Second, substantial strategic asymmetries emerge in competitive equilibrium, with payoff differentials of up to 103%. Third, under the baseline calibrated synergy scenario the model-implied upper-bound cooperation gain is 70% relative to the Nash-grounded baseline (sum of singleton coalition values = 36.87, equal to the Nash equilibrium welfare); we emphasize that this figure is parametrically determined by the assumed synergy coefficient, and a sensitivity analysis over that coefficient yields a scenario range of 35% to 105% rather than a statistically estimated effect. Malmquist-Luenberger productivity analysis reveals concerning stagnation (average index of 1.0002), with technical regression rather than advancement constraining performance. The Shapley value analysis reveals a structurally asymmetric but core-stable allocation (coefficient of variation 0.163), with the materials-tier player receiving the largest share consistent with its competitive dominance. The research provides a rigorous methodological framework for analyzing strategic-operational interactions, offers empirical evidence that challenges assumptions about competitive efficiency in technology supply chains, and delivers actionable mechanisms for implementing value-creating collaborative strategies. These findings have immediate implications for supply chain optimization, innovation policy, and the design of fair benefit-sharing mechanisms in network production systems.

Title: Building resilient product portfolios in B2B manufacturing: A multi-criteria decision-making framework for managing disruptive factors
Authors: Till Gramberg, Aron Burgel, Andreas Eggert, Thomas Bauernhansl
Abstract: This study develops a methodologically grounded decision-support framework for product portfolio management (PPM) in manufacturing business-to-business (B2B) firms, aimed at systematically addressing the growing challenges posed by disruptive change, particularly those arising from digital and sustainable transformations. A preliminary study and systematic literature review reveal that current evaluation approaches fall short in addressing these emerging challenges. To address this gap, the proposed PPM-specific framework integrates established multi-criteria decision-making (MCDM) methods: the analytic hierarchy process (AHP), the decision-making trial and evaluation laboratory (DEMATEL), and the weighted sum model (WSM). In addition to the three established PPM target dimensions – value maximization, strategic fit, and balance – the proposed methodology introduces a fourth dimension: resilience to disruptive factors. This expanded framework enables a structured derivation and weighting of evaluation criteria, identification of interdependencies within the product portfolio, and a systematic assessment of the strategic value contribution of individual portfolio elements. A case study with a global automation technology provider and evaluation workshops with three additional globally operating B2B industrial firms demonstrate the framework's practical relevance. The results indicate enhanced transparency, more objective decision-making, and systematic portfolio governance. This research contributes a formal and transparent decision support tool that facilitates strategically robust portfolio design in times of disruptive transformation, thereby addressing critical gaps in existing literature.

Title: Impact of return shipping insurance in live-streaming retailing
Authors: Yan Zhou, Xue Zhao, Shuai Liu, Feng Tao
Abstract: The growing prevalence of return shipping insurance (RSI) in live-streaming commerce presents a critical strategic dilemma. While RSI can stimulate demand by lowering consumers’ return costs, it simultaneously increases the seller’s operational costs and return rates. This paper develops an analytical framework to examine the impact of RSI in two dominant modes: self-operated and third-party live-streaming sales. We derive equilibrium outcomes with and without RSI and compare them to uncover its impacts. Our findings indicate that the seller chooses to provide RSI only under specific conditions: when the product dissatisfaction rate is high, but consumer sensitivity to return costs remains low. This finding suggests that offering RSI does not necessarily signal high product quality. Moreover, the effect of RSI on promotional effort is highly mode-dependent. In self-operated live-streaming, RSI may lead to lower seller effort for most cases, as the accompanying rise in return rates diminishes the marginal benefit of aggressive promotion. In contrast, third-party streamers, who do not bear RSI or return-related costs, are incentivized to increase effort to capitalize on heightened consumer demand. Additionally, in both modes, the introduction of RSI does not necessarily lead to higher prices. In fact, when RSI significantly raises return rates and reduces effective demand, sellers may strategically lower prices to stimulate orders. These insights provide valuable guidance for sellers and streamers in understanding RSI and designing RSI strategies aligned with their operational models and market environments.

Title: A decision support system to dynamically align supplier portfolio management decisions and actions across levels and time horizons
Authors: Pamela Danese, Marco Formentini, Pietro Romano, Marco Boem
Abstract: Supplier portfolio management is essential for organizations to achieve their strategic goals. However, there is a lack of decision support systems (DSSs) that can support purchasing managers simultaneously at the strategic, tactical and operational levels, while ensuring consistency of supplier portfolio management decisions and actions across different levels and time horizons. Existing DSSs based on purchasing portfolio models (PPMs) are static and typically address supplier or purchasing category segmentation and analysis at a single point in time. Following a design science paradigm, we specified, implemented, and evaluated NorthStar, a novel DSS for supplier portfolio management designed to align decisions and actions across levels and time horizons through a structured three-step procedure. Ex-ante and ex-post evaluations, conducted in both artificial and naturalistic settings, demonstrate the novelty, relevance, and utility of this artifact. Our study contributes to the theoretical debate at the intersection of supplier portfolio management, PPMs and DSSs, and sourcing strategy literatures. First, it demonstrates how a PPM-based DSS can align supplier portfolio decisions and actions across multiple levels, as well as across time horizons, while remaining consistent with category strategies. Second, it addresses the static nature of traditional PPMs by supporting a shift toward dynamic models that enable continuous monitoring and adaptation. Third, NorthStar operationalizes key theoretical constructs, such as dependence by suppliers, competition, and supplier portfolio complexity, translating them into measurable indicators within a structured decision process, thereby bridging theory and practice. Finally, it provides a flexible, data-driven procedure that enhances the applicability of portfolio approaches in real-world settings.

Title: Scalable state change detection for stimulus-aware digital twins
Authors: Abhishek Tiwari, Vibhor Pandhare
Abstract: One of the fundamental functionalities of a Digital Twin of any production system is its ability to serve as a ‘twin’, i.e. effective synchronization between the physical state and the digital state. This ability of being stimulus-aware through effective detection of state change forms the foundation to realistically model production behavior in real-time for improved production planning, simulation, execution, and management. Application-based top-down approaches to developing Digital Twins generally consider pre-calculated states or known data conditions, limiting their scope. In contrast, real-life production presents a myriad of possible states. Thus, a bottom-up scalable state change detection method and a systematic four-phase learning framework using minimal data are proposed for realizing stimulus-aware Digital Twins at the beginning of equipment operation. The proposed solution uses two-stage pattern recognition and change detection learning using a single state, followed by new state detection and adaptation using a novel implementation of a custom loss function to maximize the distribution discrepancy between the latent representation of the two states. Validation is performed over three experimental datasets, including a newly created gearbox dataset that varies in type of equipment, signal, operating parameters, etc. 80 experiments are conducted across different scenarios and repeated five times each, along with statistical testing to benchmark performance with the traditional approach. The proposed method detects a change in state with over 97.5% accuracy and an F1 score of more than 95.2%, irrespective of the dataset or the states used for modeling, narrowing the gap between localized success stories and the large-scale use of Digital Twins in production industries.

Title: Channel strategy to launch community group-buying channels for instant retail platforms
Authors: Chenchen Zhao, Jianghua Wu, Zepeng Wang
Abstract: Community group-buying, based on pre-sales and self-pickup, has rapidly expanded in recent years, posing a challenge to the instant retail mode, which is characterized by online ordering and instant store delivery. This study investigates whether an instant retail platform should introduce a community group-buying channel and, if so, whether it should adopt a self-run or third-party mode. In the self-run mode, employees hired by the platform serve as group leaders, with the platform determining their effort levels and paying fixed wages. Conversely, the third-party mode involves recruiting residents or community stores as group leaders, with the platform paying commissions. Although community group-buying utilizes group leaders to address the last-mile delivery issue and reduce operating costs, consumers have a higher acceptance of instant retail channels because of their superior delivery efficiency and product freshness. Our findings reveal that the platform considers introducing a self-run group-buying channel when consumer acceptance of group-buying channels is extremely high or low. When consumer acceptance is moderate, the platform prefers to establish a third-party group-buying channel if the commission rate is low; otherwise, it does not establish a group-buying channel. Interestingly, under a high commission rate and moderate consumer acceptance of group-buying, the group leader in the third-party mode may exert more effort than in the self-run mode. Furthermore, the platform's optimal commission rate initially increases and then decreases as consumer acceptance of group-buying channels increases.

Title: Supply strategies in live stream supply chains: The role of market overlap
Authors: Shaofu Du, Yuzhu Guo, Junsong Bian, Xiaolong Guo
Abstract: Selling in live-stream channels can stimulate market demand by providing lower prices than manufacturers’ online channels. Cooperating with streamers can bring extra markets for manufacturers. However, manufacturers should pay slotting fees to streamers before cooperating, and they may face market overlap and competition. One way to alleviate competition is to control the quantity of products for streamers. We develop an analytical model consisting of an online store channel operated by the manufacturer and a live-stream channel that may run out of stock operated by the streamer. Firstly, the results show that the manufacturer should base the quantity decision on the market overlap between the manufacturer and the streamer. When the market overlap is sufficiently low, the manufacturer should supply the streamer with an adequate quantity of product to enlarge the streamer’s market. When the market overlap is sufficiently high, the manufacturer should supply the streamer with a limited quantity of products to promote consumer transfer. Secondly, the results show that as the slotting fee increases, the manufacturer requires a lower market overlap if cooperating with the streamer. Finally, we extend our basic model to the Nash Bargaining scenario. Negotiation will decrease consumer surplus, but increase social welfare compared to the basic model.

Title: Integrating returnable and disposable packaging to balance efficiency, resilience, and sustainability in automotive supply chains
Authors: Jesús García-Arca, Mar Vazquez-Noguerol, Borja Ponte, J. Carlos Prado-Prado
Abstract: : The adoption of returnable packaging systems (RPSs) is widespread in supply chains across many industries due to their potential economic and environmental benefits. However, designing and managing RPSs effectively remains challenging, particularly in volatile, uncertain, and disruption-prone environments such as the automotive sector. To better understand these challenges, we conduct an exploratory analysis involving professionals from one of Europe’s largest automotive assembly plants. Drawing on the insights gathered, we develop an empirically grounded simulation model that captures the dynamics of these closed-loop supply chains (CLSCs). The model integrates the RPS with an alternative, non-returnable packaging system (NPS), used as a contingency when returnable items are not available. Through designed experiments, we investigate the operational and economic behaviour of this hybrid packaging system, demonstrating its potential as an effective strategy for achieving both efficient, sustainable and resilient supply chains. The study further shows that determining the optimal quantity of returnable packaging items is a complex decision shaped by the interplay of costs, defective item rates, disruption probabilities, and renewal policies. Interestingly, intermediate renewal periods can outperform more frequent replacement cycles in terms of total packaging costs, highlighting the need for a balanced and integrated approach to packaging management.

Title: Note on abundance or scarcity for the Wicksellian production function, or, When does an AC-curve become U-shaped?
Authors: Robert W. Grubbström
Abstract: This note attempts to find conditions for the average cost curve to have a U-shape for problems applying the Wicksellian production function (most often called the Cobb-Douglas function ) in combination with limits in the supplies of production factors. This function enables explicit solutions to be found. On the road towards conclusions, it was found that each factor could be ranked conveniently by an abundance index defined as its factor price, multiplied by its limit amount, and divided by the value of its weight parameter. This enables an ordered sequence of critical output volumes to be defined and found, at which levels the factor amounts meet their available limits, respectively. It is demonstrated that in order for an AC -curve to have a U-shape, there must be at least one production factor with limited supplies, and that the remaining non-limited factors have weights such that their sum complies with diminishing returns to scale (sum of weights being less than unity). A reasoning on the effect that scarcity has on fixed costs and thereby on competition rounds off this note.

Title: Partial understanding or full comprehension: Should platform deploy large language model to bridge consumer perception biases?
Authors: Gang Du, Yifang Ding, Zhipeng Wang, Xiaohang Yue
Abstract: Leveraging large language model (LLM) to help consumers interpret high-tech digital product information creates both opportunities and challenges for supply chain operations. While LLMs can simplify complex terms and boost purchase intent among undervaluing consumers through personalized recommendations, they may also lower the willingness to pay of those who overvalue the digital product. To examine these effects, we model a dual-channel digital product supply chain comprising a supplier with its own offline retailer and a platform retailer who decides whether to invest in LLM, while the supplier selects between reselling and agency selling modes. Our analysis yields three principal insights. First, as consumers’ underestimation of digital products deepens, the adoption of LLM leads to higher online price and demand while simultaneously suppressing offline price and demand, yet total market demand and supply chain total revenue both increase with the degree of undervaluation. Second, we derive the precise conditions under which the platform retailer derives benefit from LLM adoption, revealing that even when consumers overestimate product value, provided that overestimation remains modest, LLM adoption can still spur aggregate demand and enhance online revenues despite reducing offline demand, and the supplier is able to exploit cross channel externalities to free-ride on the platform retailer’s LLM investment and achieve revenue gains regardless of selling mode. Third, we demonstrate that under LLM adoption the supplier’s optimal choice between reselling and agency selling modes depends not only on the commission rate in the agency selling but also critically on the magnitude of consumer valuation biases.

Title: Analyzing barriers to AI-HI integration for food loss and waste reduction: A multi-actor study of food supply chains
Authors: Zhengyan Yang, Wei Zhong Wang, Yu Chen, Dursun Delen, Muhammet Deveci
Abstract: The integration of artificial intelligence (AI) and human intelligence (HI) has significant potential to reduce food loss and waste in food supply chains (FSCs), yet its implementation is hindered by socio-technical barriers whose interdependencies and actor-specific implications remain insufficiently understood. This study analyses barriers to AI-HI integration for food loss and waste reduction from a multi-actor FSC perspective. Drawing on socio-technical systems theory, a multidimensional barrier system is developed from the literature and refined through fuzzy Delphi expert elicitation. To account for uncertainty and hesitation in expert judgments, an interval-valued T-spherical fuzzy weighted Heronian mean aggregation procedure is used to derive collective assessments. The interdependent relationships among barriers are examined using the interval-valued T-spherical fuzzy-WINGS method, and a WISP-Borda decision framework is applied to assess the performance of four representative FSC actor groups in addressing these barriers. Sensitivity and comparative analyses indicate stable and consistent results. The findings identify “privacy and cybersecurity-related concerns” as the most salient barrier to AI-HI integration and reveal heterogeneous coping capabilities across FSC actors.
